anatomy.lede: Almost all of a bobbit worm stays out of sight. What shows above the sand is a head built for one thing: seizing a fish in a fraction of a second.

hotspots.label: Antennae
hotspots.text: Five striped antennae stand up from the head. They are thought to detect prey, and some worms twitch an antenna in a worm-like way that may lure fish closer.

hotspots.label: Jaws
hotspots.text: The curved grey jaws are strong, toothed plates called maxillae, carried on a pharynx that the worm can turn inside out to grab prey.

hotspots.label: Jaw tip
hotspots.text: The jaws are armed with sharp teeth. Bobbit worms are known to bite people and can cause severe wounds.

hotspots.label: Iridescent skin
hotspots.text: The body surface shimmers blue and green in the light. Related giant Eunice worms are also described as iridescent when alive.

hotspots.label: Body segments
hotspots.text: The body is a long chain of segments. In a related giant species, one incomplete specimen nearly a metre long had 520 bristle-bearing segments.

hotspots.label: Side lobe
hotspots.text: Each segment carries a small fleshy side lobe, a parapodium, with bristles; further back, feathery gills grow from them.

hotspots.label: Burrow mouth
hotspots.text: The rest of the worm lies in a mucus-lined burrow. When it pulls back, sliding sand leaves a small crater that marks the spot.

senses.lede: A buried ambush hunter needs to know exactly when something edible is overhead. Touch and sight seem to do most of the work.

senses.name: Antennae
senses.text: By day the worm attacks when its antennae are touched by passing prey. In early field tests, only a lure that moved like a living fish set off a strike.

senses.name: Eyes
senses.text: Two eyes sit on the head. At night even a diver's torch beam can trigger an attack, which suggests sight plays a part.

senses.name: Vibration
senses.text: A closely related giant Eunice from Australia retreats quickly into its burrow when it senses vibration, which makes it very hard to collect.

body.lede: The bobbit worm's body is little more than a long, muscular tube with a deadly front end.

systems.title: A pharynx that turns inside out
systems.text: To feed, the worm shoots out its pharynx and closes its strong toothed maxillae on the prey, then drags it, still alive, down into the sediment.

systems.title: Mucus mortar
systems.text: The burrow is lined with mucus. Fossil burrows thought to be from similar worms are rich in iron, probably because bacteria feeding on the mucus left iron minerals behind.

systems.title: Moving by waves
systems.text: Burrowing worms like this move mainly by waves of muscle contraction along the body, which leaves a smooth-walled tunnel.

mind.lede: A worm has a simple nervous system, but the bobbit worm's ambush is precise, and some of its prey have learned to fight back.

studies.title: Mobbed by young fish
studies.text: Over 90 dives in Indonesia's Lembeh Strait, researchers recorded 54 encounters in which groups of up to seven young monocle bream harassed bobbit worms. The mobbing lasted from 4 to 62 seconds.

studies.title: Water jets at the burrow
studies.text: The fish squirted jets of water at the burrow. Most of the time the worm did not react, but in about a quarter of cases it pulled back completely, and it never caught a mobbing fish.

studies.title: Only moving bait works
studies.text: In preliminary trials, the worms struck only at a lure that moved like a living fish, not at still bait.

studies.title: Two ways to hunt
studies.text: Mature worms keep a permanent burrow and wait for prey, while some use an antenna to imitate a wriggling worm and draw fish within reach.

survival.lede: Little is known about what eats a bobbit worm. Its main defence is simply staying hidden.

tactics.title: Living underground
tactics.text: Keeping almost the whole body in the burrow protects the worm while it waits for prey.

tactics.title: Instant retreat
tactics.text: When harassed, the worm can pull its antennae, or its whole head, back into the sand.

tactics.title: Hard to spot
tactics.text: Bobbit worms are spread thinly: only four were found in 15,000 square metres of seabed at the Lembeh Strait study site.
